label: הרב פנחס קהתי – הפקיד מהבנק שחולל מהפכה בעולם התורה

questions.question: True or false: Pinchas Kehati's original name was Pinchas Hechtman.
questions.explanation: He was born in 1910 in a village near Rovno. His father, Kehat, was a Trisk Hasid and a fervent Zionist of the "Mizrachi" movement.

questions.question: Why did he change his surname to Kehati?
options: To commemorate his father's name, Kehat, since he had only daughters
Because the Mandate authorities required it
After his teacher at the yeshiva
questions.explanation: His parents and most of his family perished in the Holocaust. The name also sounded more modern and Israeli to him.

questions.question: At which institution in Warsaw did he receive a matriculation certificate and a teaching certificate?
questions.explanation: The combination of Torah study and a matriculation certificate was unusual in the Orthodox landscape of the time.

questions.question: In which religious youth movement in Poland was he a member of the national executive?
questions.explanation: He coordinated seminars for guides who prepared youth for aliyah, a model of a "religious pioneer" that combines labor and halakha.

questions.question: True or false: Kehati completed a full degree in mathematics at the Hebrew University.
questions.explanation: He studied for one year mathematics, physics, philosophy, and Kabbalah, and was forced to stop for lack of means.

questions.question: Where did Kehati work for many years?
options: At the Ministry of Education, as an inspector
At the Tel Aviv municipality, as an engineer
At a publishing house, as an editor
At Bank Hapoel HaMizrachi, as a clerk and auditor
questions.explanation: He was known for his precision and his talent for unraveling accounting tangles, and he brought the same precision to his commentary on the Mishnah.

questions.question: True or false: Kehati was one of the founders of Bnei Akiva and a member of its first national executive.
questions.explanation: In 1937, alongside Rabbi Moshe Zvi Neria. For many years he coordinated the movement's guidance department.

questions.question: What led Kehati to write the commentary himself?
options: The sample commentaries he received missed the mark, and his wife Rachel told him to write it himself
Bnei Akiva assigned him the task by lottery
The bank requested a booklet for its savers
questions.explanation: "If you know so well what you want, write it yourself." Rachel was the "engine and fuel" of the enterprise.

questions.question: For whom was the commentary originally intended?
options: For youths who went out to work after eighth grade and were cut off from Torah study
questions.explanation: He imagined small booklets that could be carried in a pocket and studied in a queue or on the bus.

questions.question: In what form was the commentary first published?
options: In weekly booklets sent by mail to about 5,000 subscribers
questions.explanation: Each booklet contained 14 elucidated mishnayot, halakhot from the Shulchan Arukh and from the Rambam, and a passage from the Tanakh. His daughters helped with copying and mailing.

questions.question: True or false: Kehati wrote the commentary in Aramaic, in the manner of the classical commentators.
questions.explanation: He wrote in contemporary, fluent Hebrew, within reach of everyone.

questions.question: What was the main innovation in the form of the commentary?
options: A commentary on the Talmud instead of the Mishnah
Weaving the words of explanation into the text of the Mishnah, for continuous reading
questions.explanation: The learner does not need to skip between the Mishnah and the explanation: the two are read as a single unit.

questions.question: True or false: Kehati personally vocalized all six orders of the Mishnah.
questions.explanation: This was pioneering philological work, part of the effort to make the Mishnah accessible.

questions.question: Which tune of Kehati's won first place at the first Hasidic Song Festival, in 1969?
questions.explanation: He composed it in honor of the wedding of his daughter Livia. In all, he composed more than twenty tunes.

questions.question: True or false: Kehati asked to be called "Rabbi" and was strict about the title.
questions.explanation: He objected to being called "Rabbi" and did not use his teaching certificate. He attributed his success to divine assistance.

questions.question: When did Kehati die?
options: On Yom Kippur, at the age of 70
On the night of the sixth candle of Hanukkah, at the age of 66
On Lag BaOmer, at the age of 60
On the Ninth of Av, at the age of 66
questions.explanation: On 29 Kislev 5737. The number six accompanied him: the six orders of the Mishnah, the age of 66, and the sixth candle.

questions.question: How did Kehati test whether the elucidation he had written was comprehensible?
options: He sent it to a committee of rabbis
He taught it in a class at Bnei Akiva
He woke his daughters at night to check whether they understood
He compared it with the Rambam's commentary
questions.explanation: If they understood, the commentary was clear enough. He also memorized the mishnayot from a notebook of word initials.

questions.question: What did Kehati explain when, one evening, he searched for an error of one agora in his accounts?
options: That the bank would deduct it from his salary
That every agora belongs to charity
That the error shows he did something during the day and does not remember it
questions.explanation: It was not the sum that troubled him, but what it taught about his attention to all of his actions.

questions.question: On whom does Kehati's commentary rely?
options: On the Rambam, Rabbi Ovadia of Bartenura, and Tosafot Yom Tov, without personal interpretation
On the Zohar and the writings of the Ari
questions.explanation: In addition, it condenses the Gemara's innovations relating to the Mishnah and cites the halakhic ruling.

questions.question: Which enterprise's author testified that he began it inspired by Kehati?
options: The Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah
"HaMishnah HaSedura" (The Arranged Mishnah) of Rabbi Dordak
questions.explanation: Kehati created a new genre of modern, clear elucidations, which also paved the way for the Steinsaltz commentary on the Talmud.
